title: From the Original Meaning to Today: Bridging the Gap
subtitle: A practical guide to the principlizing bridge in biblical interpretation, how to move from what a text meant to its first readers to what it means for us, crossing the gap between the ancient world and today without distorting either

sections.title: The Gap Is Real
sections.body:
Between you and the text there is a canyon. The Bible was written to people who herded sheep, fought with swords, lived under emperors, and built parapets around flat roofs. You commute, you scroll, you live under a republic, your roof is pitched and railless. The distance is real, and pretending it is not real is the source of half the bad application in the church.

You cannot apply a text to today until you have honestly faced how far today is from then.

Some preachers ignore the gap and drag the ancient command straight into the present, telling people to obey a rule written for a vanished world. Others stare at the gap and conclude the text has nothing to say to us at all. Both are wrong. There is a bridge across the canyon, a disciplined way to carry the text's meaning from their world to ours without distorting either side. Learning to walk that bridge is the last and most important step in handling Scripture. Everything before it is study. This is where study becomes a word for a living person.

sections.title: Find What It Meant to Them
sections.body:
The bridge has a starting side, and you may not skip it. Before a text can mean anything to you, you have to know what it meant to them. What was the author saying to his first readers, in their situation, facing their problem.

This is the half the eager preacher rushes past. He wants the application before he has earned it, and so he builds the bridge on air.

You cannot carry a meaning across the canyon until you have a meaning to carry. So you do the work first. You read the passage in its context, in the flow of the book, in the situation that called it forth. You ask what the original readers heard, what need it met, what it told them about God and themselves. Only when you can state plainly what the text meant on its own bank do you have something solid to send across. Skip this and your application will be your own idea wearing a verse as a costume. Do this, and the rest of the bridge has a foundation under it.

sections.title: Climb to the Principle
sections.body:
Now you climb. From the specific ancient command you rise to the timeless principle underneath it, the truth about God and his ways that the specific command was expressing. This is the high point of the bridge, and it is what actually crosses the canyon.

The particulars belonged to them. The principle belongs to everyone, because it flows from the unchanging character of God.

Take the command to build a parapet around your roof so blood is not on your house if someone falls. You do not have a flat roof. But the principle is plain. God holds you responsible for the foreseeable dangers on your property and cares about your neighbor's life. That truth is as binding now as it was then. You find the principle by asking why God gave this command, what about him it reveals, what enduring concern stands behind the time bound particular. The principle is broad enough to span the centuries and specific enough to still carry weight. It is the load bearing arch of the whole bridge.

sections.title: Come Down Into Today
sections.body:
Then you descend the far side. You take the timeless principle and ask what it requires in your own world, with your own particulars. The principle does not stay in the air. It lands, concretely, in a real life that looks nothing like the original.

So you fence the pool. You salt the icy steps. You fix the broken railing before a guest falls. The parapet has reached your house.

This is where many go wrong by stopping too high, content with a vague principle that never costs anything. Love your neighbor, they say, and leave it floating. The bridge is not finished until the principle touches ground in a specific, livable obedience for actual people in your pews. And the new particulars must fit your world the way the old ones fit theirs, expressing the same truth in a different setting. Down off the bridge, into the kitchen and the office and the driveway, the ancient word arrives, changed in form, identical in heart. That is a faithful application.

sections.title: Guardrails on the Bridge
sections.body:
A few guardrails keep you from falling off. The principle you climb to must actually arise from the text, not be smuggled in from your own agenda. If you can make a passage support a point its author would not recognize, you have not crossed the bridge. You have wandered off it.

And the principle must fit the whole of Scripture. A true principle from one text will never contradict the clear teaching of the rest.

Watch also that you do not flatten every text into the same handful of safe principles, so that every passage somehow means be nice and trust God. The Bible is richer than that, and lazy bridging robs it. Test your application by asking whether your first readers would recognize it as the same truth they were given, dressed for a new day. Run it past the rest of the canon. Hold it loosely enough to be corrected. These guardrails are not restrictions on freedom. They are what keep the bridge over the canyon instead of dropping you into it.

sections.title: Do Not Stop on the Bridge
sections.body:
So this is the whole motion. Find what it meant to them. Climb to the principle that flows from God's character. Come down into a real obedience for today, guarded by the text and the canon. Then take the next step, which is the only one that finally matters. Do it.

A bridge you build and never cross is just a monument. The point was never to admire the principle. It was to obey it.

I have preached sermons that walked the bridge beautifully and stopped at the railing, leaving everyone informed and no one changed. That is a failure dressed as faithfulness. The reason we cross from the ancient text to the present moment is so that the word that came to them comes to us, and lands, and costs us something, and bends our actual lives toward God. Do the study. Climb to the principle. Come all the way down. And then walk off the bridge into your real life and live what you found. That is what reading the Bible was always for.
